newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanians on strike to protest higher prices.
newsitem.headline: Albanians on strike to protest higher prices.

text.p: Tens of thousands of Albanians staged a one-hour warning strike on Monday, demanding full compensation from the government for recent price hikes in basic goods and rising inflation, union officials said.
"The warning strike aims at drawing the attention of the people and the government to our problems," Estref Mersinaj of the Independent Trade Union told Reuters.
Mersinaj said workers wanted compensation for higher bread, gas and kerosene prices after those were liberalised by the conservative government of President Sali Berisha last July.
They also want to be reimbursed for inflation gains after the introduction of a new tariff system and value-added tax.
Bread prices have been a sensitive issue since Albania toppled its hardline communist regime in 1990. More than 40 people were killed in a wave of food riots in 1991.

Workers in the areas of education, health care, telecommunications, transport and in Albania's light industry participated in Monday's protests, organised by the Independent Trade Union jointly with the Confederation of Albanian Trade Unions, the reformed heirs to the ex-communist trade unions.

The government supplements the income of all public sector employees and pensioners with subsidies of 150-250 leks (about $17-28) per month to compensate for any rise in bread prices, but trade unions say that was not enough. "We want 100 percent compensation," Mersinaj said.
An official of the Confederation of Trade Unions said workers may stage a one-day strike next week if the government does not respond to their demands.

Imported wheat and flour are still excluded from both customs tariffs and value-added tax while bakeries continue to receive subsidies for electricity, water and fuel, but the introduction VAT and a new customs law has significantly increased most other prices in the small Balkan nation.
Albania's consumer prices rose 16.1 percent in August compared to the same month the previous year and were up 1.9 percent from the month before.
The government still controls prices of electricity, petrol and water.
